title: Reading the Rows: Five Measurement Defects in an Audit of an Answer Endpoint, and the One Result That Remained
description: A published number about a commercial data product is a property of the harness that produced it until someone has looked below the number. This paper is one worked case. I built an instrument that measures how often an API affirms a false claim about a named person, with ground truth taken from SEC Section 16 filings and OpenAlex authorship records. It produced six headline numbers. Five were defects of my measurement: a query packed into the wrong field, a filter that returned the answer, a parser that read names out of page titles, negatives that were true, and an estimator that forced a monotone shape onto a curve that is not monotone. None was visible in the number itself; each surfaced when I read the returned rows or the binned data underneath. The sixth, a corrected version of the fourth, survived three checks of my own design. Asked whether a named researcher has published in a topic, one endpoint (Exa /answer, one prompt, September 2026) confirmed 0.9600 of attested claims and affirmed claims that have no matching work in the author's OpenAlex record at 0.1680 for an adjacent subfield, 0.1320 for an adjacent field and 0.0840 for a wholly different domain (n=250 per stratum; 95% Wilson intervals [0.1268,0.2193], [0.0956,0.1796], [0.0556,0.1250]). The different-domain rate is not zero, but a single-reader, unblinded reading of all 21 of its affirmations finds only 6 clearly the endpoint's error; the rest are broad topic labels or work that may belong to the author under another profile, so the rates are upper bounds that carry an oracle error of unknown size. The endpoint's schema-elicited confidence sits at ceiling and does not beat a constant forecast. The result describes one endpoint, one prompt and one window, drawn once, and the ground truth is partly a third-party classifier's output. I claim nothing about the vendor's other products, about other vendors, or about people-search indexes, whose arm stayed unmeasured after five budgets. I also list the defects I found in this repository while preparing the paper. Code, results and pre-registrations are public. Not peer reviewed. Code and protocol: https://github.com/caiotheodoro/titer
